newsitem.title: USA: Wall Street seen opening mixed to lower.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street seen opening mixed to lower.

text.p: Wall Street stocks are expected to open mixed to lower Wednesday, weighed down by warnings on results from several key high-technology companies.
"It's going to be a high-tech challenge, and high tech has a very important effect on the proceedings," said Larry Wachtel, a market analyst at Prudential Securities.

After the market closed Tuesday, Gateway 2000 Inc, a direct marketer of personal computers, said it expected revenues for the second quarter to be flat compared with the first quarter's $1.42 billion because of weaker-than-expected demand.

Gateway's comments were followed by Seagate Technology Inc's second results forecast in two weeks. Seagate said its fourth-quarter revenues would be $2.0-$2.1 billion, basically flat compared with a year earlier.
Seagate, a disk drive maker, said weak demand for its high-end products would have a "significant" impact on earnings. In after-hours trading the stock shed about five points to $29.625
Oracle Corp, the database software giant, posted fourth-quarter earnings that met analysts' expectations but disappointed some investors who had hpoed for even better results.
The 30-year bond was off 3/32 with its yield at 6.73 percent. The Standard & Poor's index futures were down 2.45 to 900.30.
Japan's Nikkei average closed lower, down 95.81 points, or 0.47 percent, at 20,497.85. In London, the FTSE 100 was down 39.9 points at 4652.3.
U.S. stocks were lower in London, weighed down by weak technology issues.
The dollar moved higher against the yen, trading at 113.55/65 yen. In Europe the dollar was trading at 1.7261/66 marks.

The New York Times said in its Market Place column that Tele-Communications Inc's complex agreement to buy back a block of stock owned by TCI's late founder, Bob Magness, was received favorably by Wall Street.
The Wall Street Journal said in its Heard on the Street column that humor on Wall Street has hit a bear market, chilled by sexual harassment lawsuits and a new culture emerging on trading floors.
